paras: The lynching of Thomas Sayers took place near Bramwell, Mercer County, West Virginia, around the beginning of November 1888, when a mob took Sayers, a Black man accused of leading a highway robbery, from officers taking him to jail and hanged him from a tree. He had been held for the grand jury after an attack on four white produce sellers in which two were shot. A Post-Dispatch wire carried the news nationally under headlines such as "Negro Murderer Lynched," though reports differed on the date, on whether the robbery victims died, and on how many men were lynched.

According to dispatches from Bramwell, A. H. Lilly, a farmer, and three neighbors took a wagonload of produce to Simmons Creek, about a mile below Bramwell, on Saturday, October 27, and sold it, "realizing quite a sum of money."

On Sunday, October 28, as the men started home, they were waylaid by what the papers called a "band of negroes"; two of them were shot and robbed, and the other two escaped and gave the alarm at Bramwell. A Charleston dispatch of October 31 said the gang "shot and killed two" and took $600, and named the survivors Henderson and Johnson. Fifty men went in pursuit, and the Washington Evening Star wrote that the men sought "will be lynched if caught."

A posse arrested Thomas Sayers, described as the gang's "ring-leader," on Monday night or Tuesday by differing accounts. After a preliminary examination before a justice at Bramwell, Sayers was ordered to jail in default of $5,000 bail to await the action of the grand jury. Before the guards reached the jail, according to the South Branch Intelligencer, "a mob set upon them and captured Sayers, whom they swung to a tree by the road-side." A Bramwell dispatch to the Wheeling Intelligencer said that "Great excitement prevailed" and that "a mob of unknown men" took him.

The South Branch Intelligencer reported that officers were pursuing the rest of the gang, who "if caught they will suffer the fate of their leader," and that the people were "thoroughly aroused" and meant to "put down lawlessness in Mercer county." No report of an inquest, of arrests of members of the mob, or of any later capture of the other men sought appears in the coverage.

Most papers learned of the lynching through a Post-Dispatch special from Charleston, which called Sayers "one of the negro highwaymen who murdered and robbed two peddlers." It ran on November 2 and 3 from Washington and New York to Savannah, San Antonio and Sacramento under headlines such as "Lynched for His Crime," "Negro Murderer Lynched," and the New York Evening World's "Thomas Sayers, a Negro, Lynched." The copying introduced errors: the Evening World datelined its item "Charleston, S. C.," the New York Sun spelled the name "Savers," and the Wheeling Intelligencer's condensed telegram put Mercer County in "Mo."

The robbery had first appeared under headlines such as "Waylaid by Negro Bandits" and "Murdered by Negro Highwaymen," and some weeklies still printed only that report as late as November 10, while others reduced the lynching to a line or two through mid-November.

The fuller West Virginia accounts, from Bramwell and the South Branch Intelligencer, described the arrest, hearing and bail before the hanging, and the Wheeling Intelligencer headed its Bramwell dispatch "A Man Concerned in a Robbery and Murder Pays the Penalty." None gave an account from Sayers or evidence against him beyond the charge.

The Post-Dispatch wire dated the lynching Wednesday night, October 31, but its Evening Star version said "last night" and other briefs said November 2. The local accounts point later still: the South Branch Intelligencer put the hearing on Thursday evening, November 1, and a Bramwell dispatch of November 4 said Sayers was caught "yesterday evening."

The Charleston wires said two travellers were killed or "murdered," but the Bramwell accounts said only that two were shot. The robbery was placed at Flipping Creek in some reports and at Simmons Creek in the Bramwell accounts.
A Christiansburg dispatch to the Richmond Dispatch alone reported that "three negroes were lynched this week for highway robbery" at "Flippo," near Bramwell; every other account names one man.

Sayers was seized from officers by 'a mob of unknown men' and hanged without trial (A12, A18, A24) in retaliation for a robbery and shooting he was accused of leading (A24); the wire calls it 'lynched' (A10).

Independent dispatches from Bramwell (A12, A18), the South Branch Intelligencer (A24), the Post-Dispatch Charleston special (A10, A8) and a Christiansburg correspondent (A13) all report the lynching, though they differ on date and number.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Post-Dispatch item verbatim, calling Sayers a 'negro' highwayman and murderer under headlines like 'Negro Murderer Lynched' and 'Lynched for His Crime'.
The South Branch Intelligencer and Wheeling Intelligencer treated the hanging as deserved: 'Pays the Penalty', and the people 'propose to put down lawlessness in Mercer county'.
The Alexandria Gazette's Bramwell special narrated the arrest, hearing and seizure without comment under 'A Robber Lynched'.

conflicts.note: The local Bramwell and South Branch accounts give a sequence (arrest, hearing, jail transfer) that puts the lynching on or after Thursday, Nov. 1, later than the wire's Wednesday; they are closer to the scene but disagree with each other on the arrest day.
Only the Christiansburg correspondent says three; all other reports name one man.
The local accounts never say the two men died.
